note.text: An inference combines textual clues with a reasonable connection. It is more than copying a sentence, but it must remain supported. Several explanations may fit the same clue, so the strength of the conclusion must match the evidence. Words such as may, suggests and probably can preserve appropriate uncertainty. An absence of information is not proof that an event never occurred.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to justify a cautious inference and distinguish it from an unstated certainty. Builds on: main ideas and summary fidelity. Leads to: character interpretation and prose.

sections.heading: Read the original model
sections.text: Original passage: Rain tapped the roof. Bih placed a basin under a damp patch and moved the books away. The passage suggests concern about water reaching the books. It does not state who owns the roof or prove that every book was damaged. The action supports an inference about precaution without establishing all background facts.

sections.heading: Apply and check
sections.text: Name the clue, explain the link and state the inference with suitable certainty. Test an alternative explanation. Reject an answer that adds a private motive or universal outcome without evidence.

cards.idea: Read the whole example before identifying its function.
example: Bih moves books away from a damp patch.
Bih may be trying to protect books from water.
The passage does not identify the roof’s owner.
A cautious reader asks whether books were moved before damage occurred.

cards.idea: A correction must preserve the intended meaning and form.
example: An inference needs no evidence from the passage. Correction: The action provides a basis for interpretation.
Concern about water proves every book is already ruined. Correction: A precaution does not prove the feared damage happened.
Missing ownership information proves nobody owns it. Correction: Unstated information remains unknown.
Only one possible motive can ever fit an action. Correction: Evidence can leave more than one explanation open.

pick.q: Original passage: Ayuk checked the clouds and placed a cover over the seed trays. Which inference is supported?
pick.r: He may be protecting the trays from expected weather
w: He certainly knows tomorrow’s rainfall total
e: No exact forecast is supplied.
Precaution does not establish destruction.
Ownership beyond the trays is not stated.
pick.y: Cloud checking and a cover support a weather precaution.

pick.q: Original passage: Before speaking, Bih read her notes again and took a slow breath. Which conclusion respects the evidence?
pick.r: She appears to be preparing carefully
e: Reading notes does not prove total forgetting.
No hostility towards listeners is stated.
No outcome has occurred in the excerpt.
pick.y: The actions support preparation, not invented certainty about feelings or outcomes.

pick.q: Original passage: The hall was dark when the group arrived. Nothing else is said. What remains uncertain?
e: Darkness is directly stated.
Arrival is directly stated.
The text explicitly describes that condition.
pick.y: A condition alone does not identify its cause.
